items.title: Going by; Laughing; Living.
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
Do you hear all this noise? It's frightening.

The sky is pink, and orange, and yellow all washed-out by the grey of the clouds.

A group of people is going by, they are laughing, they are living.

And I wonder how.

I'm trying to understand, how can I go by? How can I laugh? How can I live?

Why aren't they walking alone?

The room is getting dark, the colors have faded.

I can't hear the people anymore, but they are still walking around my brain.

They are going by, they are laughing, they are living.

Getting my head through the window, I am looking at the trees. Looking right in their eyes.

"I'm sorry", I tell them.

You didn't deserve this.

"You are precious", I tell them.

And I wonder why I don't hear it coming from everywhere.

Why is there only this scary noise?

The noise of life going on, of people going by.

As if it was all ok. As if all around us wasn't screaming.

But the noise is too loud, too loud to listen with our ears.

items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
Hi folks,

In this article I’ll share the results of ad-hoc security vulnerabilities research I’ve done on windows 8 apps deployment. Specifically, we’ll discuss fundamental design flaws that allow to Reverse Engineer Win8 apps, modification of installed apps and the negative implications on Intellectual Property rights protection, Licensing models and overall PC security. Finally we’ll discuss some creative ideas on how to mitigate these security issues. 

 

Meet the mother-load: C:\Program Files\Applications

All Windows 8 applications in the developer preview are installed under the clandestine C:\Program Files\Applications location. I will hazard a guess and say that once the Windows App Store goes online it will install all apps under that folder. Currently the folder is an invisible one and cannot be accessed from Windows Explorer user interface on a new Win8 developer preview install.

items.title: Silence
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
And then, there is the silence. The silence when you've just finished a book.

It's a weird silence, not a silence as far as sound goes. Roadwork is still roaring by the window, the fan is still humming slowly, the dog is still munching on its kibbles. But a silence of the mind.

The characters have been jumping out the pages and into your mind, each speaking with their own voice, sharing vivid images of their lives. You are somewhere with them, listening to them, and then the last page, you close the book and there's the silence.

A silence of pondering, not really knowing what to say next. The usual voice inside your mind hasn't taken its place back, it's empty and quiet.

You are left with feelings that precede thoughts. Feelings that are part your own, part those of the book. Illusions of your life pasted onto the ones of the characters.

Feelings filled of what ifs and rememberings of what could have been and what could be.

items.title: Taking Request Cancellation Beyond the Browser
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
🫧 Open on Bubbles

Imagine opening a dashboard that generates a fairly detailed analytics report. You click a button, the application starts fetching data from a couple of APIs, and then you realise you don’t need the report anymore. So, you close the tab and move on.

From your (user’s) perspective, the operation is over. But on the server, things might be very different.

It could still be making API calls , running database queries , or an expensive operation such as waiting for an AI model to generate a response . All of that work might continue even though there’s nobody waiting for the result anymore.

This is one of those small problems in web development that often goes unnoticed. We spend a lot of time making requests faster, but we don’t always think about what happens when someone no longer needs a request to finish.

Anyway, this is where request cancellation becomes interesting.

CIR is short for "Coordinator for International Relations." But in this case, I'm hired directly through my city, thanks to a sister city connection. More on that detail another time.

I think my job title makes me sound more lofty and in-charge than I am. I'm only sometimes a "coordinator," and mainly I'm an assistant to my department head, who does the actual coordination and heavy lifting when it comes to international affairs. My Japanese title is more accurate, honestly:

国際（こくさい）"kokusai" - international

交流（こうりゅう）"kouryuu" - exchange

員（いん）"in" (pronounced like "een") - employee

In a nutshell, CIRS are the incredibly few but critical representatives of their respective countries, and serve as the translators and bridges between Japan and the rest of the world.

items.title: Le futur existe-t-il ?
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
Comment envisager l'avenir ?

Enfant, nous le voyons trop loin pour être atteignable.

Adultes, nous formons des projets: mariage, enfants, maison, carrière… autant d'étapes à franchir, d'obstacles à sauter qui balisent notre chemin. Pas d'horizon !

Puis vient la vieillesse, encore quelques projets, un horizon qui se restreint, qui s'amenuise: on l'appelle l'espoir de durer. Un mur que l'on sait devoir bientôt frapper.

Somme tout, l'avenir n'existe pas ! Il n'arrive jamais !

Dès lors faut-il en conclure que cette route de tous les possibles, cet océan à l'horizon sans fin soit pur effet de notre imagination?

Qu'en dit la poésie?

Aujourd'hui, pour y répondre, abordons ce poète qui signait de son nom seul: Guillevic .

Homme de chiffres comme de lettres, il déploie, tel un paysage, une écriture, simple, directe, "rugueuse" diront certains critiques, une poésie qui interroge le monde, la nature, sa beauté comme sa rudesse, et leur rapport au langage.

items.title: 75% of Rockstar’s workers have voted against unionizing
items.label: Hobbies and Creative
items.excerpt:
The IWGB, a union representing some Rockstar workers, has confirmed that workers rejected a deal that would recognize the Rockstar Game Workers Union.

The two-week ballot, which ran from 12 to 26 November, overlapped with the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6. The results were roughly 25% in favor of recognizing the union, and 75% against, with the vast majority of its around 1,600 employees participating.

Recognition would have established a formal framework for workers to negotiate collectively over pay, overtime, bonuses, leave, pensions, and the impact of AI and redundancies.

The result does not prevent Rockstar workers from organizing with the IWGB or exercising their trade union rights, but means management will not be formally committed to regular meetings with union representatives. The union is also able to continue representing individual members.

items.title: Toasted coconut on pumpkin pie
items.label: Q&A
items.excerpt:
My family has always served pumpkin pie with whipped cream and toasted coconut. I have never met anyone else who has toasted coconut with their pumpkin pie. Where did they get this from?

Totally standard canned pumpkin, evaporated milk, eggs type pumpkin pie. I have a distinct memory of my grandmother toasting sweetened shredded coconut on a baking sheet in the oven and watching it like a hawk because it burns easily. She's no longer with us so I can't ask her. My dad, her son, has no idea. She was a great baker, but not an experimental one. Child of Polish immigrants, grew up on a farm in Connecticut during the Depression. Primarily a homemaker; later in life worked in a grocery store deli.

Internet searches have been unhelpful because they only bring up pie that uses coconut milk or oil as a dairy alternative.

Any ideas? Anyone else with this tradition? Any other interesting pumpkin pie toppings?
